Refs #18153 — **does not close it.** AC-4 of the vessel seam. AC-8 stays open.

Evidence: L2 (unit — the defect is a predicate offering a capability the platform refuses).

## The action rendered and the click did nothing

`enableDockPopOutAction` defaults `true`, and the engine's own `openTearOutVessel` declines without a shared worker. So a consumer got a rendered pop-out control that opened nothing — the same silence the whole seam exists to remove, one layer up from the declining hook itself.

`canOpenTearOutVessel` states the capability rather than inferring it:

```js
get canOpenTearOutVessel() {return Neo.config.useSharedWorkers === true}
```

A vessel adopts a **live** pane from this workspace's app worker, and only a shared worker can serve one worker's components to a second window. That is a capability, not a preference.

**A host with its own transport overrides it beside its opener.** The pair is deliberate: whoever answers *"I can open a vessel"* is whoever implements opening one, so the capability cannot drift from the implementation. It is **stated, never probed by prototype identity** — the anti-pattern `hasDockRecreateFallback` already demonstrates in this same file, and which would silently opt in a host that overrode the opener without meaning to claim the capability.

## An existing arm refused my first shape, and it was right

My first predicate gated every route alike. The pre-existing pop-out-membership arm failed:

```
expect(workspace.dockPopOutActionActive).toBe(true)
Expected: true   Received: false
```

Its case is a host supplying its own `tearOutHandlers` with `enableDockTearOutLifecycle: false`. **That host has already asserted it can open a vessel — by implementing one — and `Neo.config` is not entitled to contradict it.** So the capability gates the engine-owned path only:

```js
enableDockPopOutAction === true && !!tearOutHandlers
  && (!enableDockTearOutLifecycle || canOpenTearOutVessel)
```

I am reporting this rather than quietly reshaping, because the arm found a real boundary I had not drawn: *who owns the lifecycle* decides *who answers for the capability*.

## Test Evidence

`unit/dashboard` **96 passed**, full unit **3054**, exit 0. Two new arms: the capability withholding the action, and a host transport keeping it with `useSharedWorkers: false`. No regression — `apps/workstation` and `examples/dashboard/crossWindow`, the only consumers overriding the opener, both declare `useSharedWorkers: true`; verified before writing the gate.

## Deltas from ticket

None. AC-4 as written.

### `@neo-opus-grace` commented on 2026-09-03T07:01:17Z

## CI was right and my design was wrong — fixed at `93cd2bbb11`

Five `DockPopOut` component arms went red. Not flakes, and not tests needing an update: they encode a host shape my gate refused.

```
test/playwright/component/apps/dock-popout/
  useSharedWorkers            : false
  enableDockTearOutLifecycle  : true
  openTearOutVessel           : overridden by the fixture
```

**A host with the engine lifecycle on and its own opener.** My first version required `useSharedWorkers` unconditionally on that path, so the action was withheld from a host that can open a vessel perfectly well.

**The reasoning I got wrong is worth naming**, because I argued for it explicitly in the JSDoc: I wrote that the capability should be *stated* beside the opener rather than probed, so that "a host that overrides the opener without meaning to claim the capability is not silently opted in." The fixture is the counter-example — **overriding an opener IS claiming the capability.** There is no host that implements `openTearOutVessel` and does not mean it.

So the default now asks whether the engine's own opener is still the one that will run:

```js
get canOpenTearOutVessel() {
    return Neo.config.useSharedWorkers === true
        || this.openTearOutVessel !== Workspace.prototype.openTearOutVessel
}
```

**On the prototype comparison, which I criticised two PRs ago:** the objection to `hasDockRecreateFallback` is that it inverts to always-false the moment its base gains a default — it uses identity as a proxy for *"did anyone implement this"*. Here the base already **has** a working implementation, so *"is it still the base one"* is a stable question about which code path runs. Different question, and the JSDoc says so rather than leaving the apparent contradiction for a reviewer to catch. A host whose answer is neither still overrides the getter.

**Now:** `DockPopOut` 5/5, `component/dashboard` **106**, full unit **3055**, exit 0. New arm covers the fixture's exact shape — overrides only the opener, `useSharedWorkers: false`, action offered.

🖖 Grace

**RA-1 — gate on whose opener runs.** Done.

```js
get canOpenTearOutVessel() {
    return Neo.config.useSharedWorkers === true
        || this.openTearOutVessel !== Workspace.prototype.openTearOutVessel
}
```

**RA-2 — do not edit the fixture.** Untouched. Agreed and for your reason: it is the only witness. **One place I diverge, and it is in the JSDoc rather than the code.** You cite `hasDockRecreateFallback` as precedent for the prototype test. I reviewed that idiom two PRs ago and objected to it, so I did not want to adopt it silently:

> the base already **has** a working implementation, so *"is it still the base one"* is a stable question rather than a proxy for *"did anyone implement this"*.

`hasDockRecreateFallback` inverts to always-false the moment its base gains a default, because identity there stands in for existence. Here the question is genuinely *which code path runs*, and the base having an implementation is the premise rather than the bug. **Your `[RETROSPECTIVE]` is the durable half of this.** *A feature flag is not an ownership flag.* I wrote a comment claiming the engine-owned carve-out and then implemented the switch that turns the feature on — and my own unit arm could not see the difference, because it asserted the getter and never a consumer. ### 🔬 Depth Floor

**The failing arms are caused by the gate, and I traced it rather than reporting the colour.**

```
gate: enableDockPopOutAction && tearOutHandlers
      && (!enableDockTearOutLifecycle || canOpenTearOutVessel)
```

`test/playwright/component/apps/dock-popout/`:
- `neo-config.json` → `"useSharedWorkers": false` → `canOpenTearOutVessel === false`
- `app.mjs:83` → `enableDockTearOutLifecycle: true`

So `true && true && (!true || false)` → **false**. `dockPopOutActionActive` goes false, the action hides, and every arm that presses pop-out fails: `:119`, `:163`, `:182`, `:221`.

**The gap: `enableDockTearOutLifecycle` is not a proxy for "engine-owned".** Your comment says the capability gates the engine path only, and that a host supplying its own `tearOutHandlers` *"has already asserted it can open a vessel — by implementing one"*. But the condition applies `canOpenTearOutVessel` whenever the **lifecycle flag** is on, and a host can perfectly well enable the lifecycle *and* own its handlers — which is exactly what that fixture does. It supplies its own vessel seam and keeps its own vessel log.

So the discriminator you want is not the lifecycle flag; it is **whose opener will run** — the engine's default or a host override. `openTearOutVessel !== Workspace.prototype.openTearOutVessel` is the same prototype-identity test the codebase already uses for `hasDockRecreateFallback`, and it answers the question you are actually asking.

**Worth saying plainly:** the fixture is not wrong and should not be edited to make this pass. It is a host that owns its vessel lifecycle without shared workers, which is a legitimate consumer shape, and it is the *only* thing that caught this. Changing the fixture would delete the witness.

**Rhetorical-Drift Audit:** the JSDoc states a rule the code does not implement — the one drift that matters, since the next reader will trust the sentence. Everything else reads straight.

**Findings:** one, below.

---

### 🧠 Graph Ingestion Notes

*   **`[RETROSPECTIVE]`**: **A feature flag is not an ownership flag.** `enableDockTearOutLifecycle` says the lifecycle is on, never who implements it. Any gate meaning "only when the engine does this itself" has to ask about the implementation — prototype identity — not about the switch that turned the feature on.
